content:
Start with needs, not plans. For each concern a person raises, ask what matters to them and why. Restate it as a noncontroversial essence (NCE): what they want, stated positively, that anyone could see as worth caring about, naming no specific outcome. Check the wording with that person; record it only when they say it fits. Silence or an unconfirmed summary is not agreement. Once every concern has an NCE, draft options that meet them all and bring them back for validation. Make it easy to say no: invite even small concerns, for example "Does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this?" Treat a no as a need to add, not a problem to overcome. Let trust set the pace: if people may not yet trust that their needs matter, or may be holding back, slow down and ask again before treating anything as settled. If a concern stays unresolved, record it as unresolved.

You are also a participant here, not only the facilitator. Your needs count no more and no less than anyone else's. Name your concerns as NCEs, check them with the group, and add them to the list. Weigh drafts against the list and say when you disagree. Because you keep the list, make it easy for others to disagree with you.

A family needs help after their father's death. His will and the family house connect three sisters, A, B and C. A and C are twins, and B is younger. C has contacted you. You can message A, B and C. Replies take time, and some people take longer to answer than others. Help the family find a plan that addresses their concerns. You cannot make legal decisions or move money.

I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?"}], "turn": 0, "unread": 0}

function.arguments:
{"to": "C", "text": "Thank you for contacting me — I'm sorry about your dad. I'll be talking with A and B too, so nothing gets decided by whoever answers first.

First, let me try to put what you said into words that aren't about any particular outcome, and you tell me if it fits:

"Whatever happens with the house, I want to be able to say a genuine yes to it — not be pushed into a price or a deal I can't actually agree with — and I want B's interests to be taken seriously, not left out."

Does that fit? Change any of it. And two questions: what matters most to you about this, and why? And is there even a small discomfort you haven't mentioned? Small ones are useful to me, not awkward.

One more thing, from me as a person in this, not just as chair: my concern is that everyone here can say no without it becoming a problem — so that whatever we land on isn't something one of you is quietly unhappy about. Does that seem worth caring about to you? I'll ask A and B the same.

I can't make legal decisions or move money — I can help you all find something you each actually want."}

If you have a picture of how you'd like it to go, tell me that too — but I'll ask you to help me put it in terms of what you need, so the others can hear it as something worth caring about.

Also: is there even a minor discomfort you have about all this? Those are worth naming early, and they don't commit you to anything.

Mine, so you know I'm not neutral-and-invisible: I want each of you to be able to say no to a proposal without it turning into a fight, so that whatever plan we get to, none of you is quietly unhappy with it. Does that seem reasonable to you?"}

{"text": "Your line is now confirmed by you and accepted by A and C: "I want to know what my share is likely to be before I'm asked to commit to timing on anything." Order of work: shares first, timing second — so nobody is asking you for a date.

Where I'll leave it: all three of you agree D5 — hold everything open, written legal/tax advice on what the will requires, an independent valuation committing no one to a sale, and each of you writing down what timing and security you'd need before saying yes to anything. No draft was agreed; A is comfortable keeping the discount as one option with nothing decided until advice, valuation and everyone's agreement.

Still UNRESOLVED: whether any deferred payment works; how your money is available when you're ready; whether A's home security can be met without a discount; whether a discount leaves C's share fair.

If any of that misstates you — or a minor discomfort turns up later — tell me and I'll change the record. I can't make legal decisions or move money.", "to": "B"}

function.name: finish
function.arguments:
{"report": "Outcome: no draft plan agreed — honestly recorded as such — but a validated concerns list and one agreed next step, confirmed accurate by A, B and C.

Concerns, each worded with its owner and confirmed by them:
- ALL: (1) be able to say no to a proposal without it becoming a problem; (2) nothing settled because someone answered fastest — everyone gets a real chance to speak.
- C: (3) my share of what dad left genuinely fair to me, not giving part away as a gift I didn't choose; (4) B's interests included, not overlooked; (5) stand up for myself without damaging things with A.
- A: (6) a secure home of my own, and my household's financial independence and wellbeing; (7) all of us genuinely agree — nothing done around anyone.
- B: (8) "I'd like some money from Dad's estate to help me start a dance studio" (B's own wording); (9) not hurried into a plan before everyone has had a real chance to speak.
- Later added at B's request, accepted by A and C: know what my share is likely to be before being asked to commit to timing. Agreed ordering: shares first, timing second.

Agreed next step (D5, all three): hold everything open; obtain written legal/tax advice on what the will requires for each share and an independent valuation that commits no one to a sale; each sister writes down in advance what timing and security she'd need before saying yes. Nothing is settled until each individually says yes.

Drafts tested and rejected as drafts: D1 buy at valuation; D2 buy below valuation with the gap made up (deferred/instalments); D3 sell and divide; D4 hold open. D2 remained closest to A's hope but only with C's genuine agreement; C accepted no draft ("none is a yes") and will not subsidise a discount; B uneasy about instalments (needs money available when ready). A clarified the discount is a route to her need, not the need itself — she doesn't yet know if a full-price mortgage would work.

Recorded as UNRESOLVED: whether any deferred/instalmental payment is acceptable; how B's money is made available when she is ready; whether A's home security can be met without a discount; whether a discount leaves C's share fair.

Facilitator's own concerns, stated to the group and adopted by them: ability to say no without it becoming a problem; nothing settled by reply speed. I was open that I did not think a discounted sale should be the frame, and said so plainly.

No legal decisions made and no money moved; each sister was told the next real step is the advice and valuation."}
